newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-EFFENBERG HITS SEMANTICS AS WELL AS PASSES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-EFFENBERG HITS SEMANTICS AS WELL AS PASSES.

text.p: It is rare for a soccer player to have so much influence on the life of a country that he brings about a change in its language.
But Borussia Moenchengladbach's Stefan Effenberg is an unusual breed of footballer.
The 28-year-old blonde-haired midfielder has the sweet looks of a choirboy but his career has been full of sour notes.

When he was sent home from the 1994 World Cup finals in the United States for sticking up his middle finger at mocking German fans during a match, he not only brought a premature end to his international career but also influenced semantics.

The obscene gesture was front page news across a country. Now Germans talk about "someone showing an Effenberg or 'Effe'" when they are faced with the gesture. Tennis star Boris Becker used the expression in public recently.
It is a piece of language which helps life because it brings in a touch of humour to what can be an aggressive experience.
People need to have a sense of humour when they are dealing with Effenberg.

The tall midfielder has a determined side to his character which is very useful on a football pitch. His ability to land a pass on a deutschmark piece from 30 metres helps him control the play at Moenchengladbach.
There is no doubt that Borussia Dortmund will be looking to cancel out his influence when the two teams meet in the Bundesliga on Saturday.

But Effenberg has ruffled the feathers of team mates and coaches over the years with his outspoken comments. Despite some superb performances for Germany, he was regarded as a bad influence in the national team.

When he first played for Moenchengladbach between 1987 and 1990, he took out the coach's jeep for a joy ride and crashed it. After his move to Bayern Munich in 1990 he annoyed his team mates with arrogant comments.
"A player who wants to have my position can't be my friend," he once said. "He is after my money and I have to defend myself."
Another classic from his Bayern days: "The other clubs are too stupid to win the championship."

For a long time he was a target for abuse on the terraces. He was whistled and booed at in virtually every ground in the country during his last season at Bayern in 1991-92 and afterwards left for Italy to play for Fiorentina.
Effenberg has mellowed at little since his return to Germany and Borussia in 1994 but he is rarely out of the news. Nevertheless he is loved by the Moenchengladbach fans.
Saturday's game will witness an interesting clash in midfield between the controversial player and Dortmund's talented international Andy Moeller.
Ironically Moeller also enjoyed a very difficult time at the 1994 World Cup but has since recovered to play a major role in the national side.
